sections.heading: Coming to the God who keeps us
sections.text: Lord God, you are the one who keeps us, rules over us, saves us, and will one day judge all things. Quiet our restless hearts tonight so that we can call on you honestly and attentively. Help us not to be ruled by our appetites, our moods, or only by what we can see and feel. Teach us to trust you with a living faith.
theological_themes: God preserves and governs his people.
God is both Saviour and coming Judge.
Prayer requires dependence on God, not self-generated spirituality.
Faith looks beyond the flesh and the senses to God himself.

scripture_references.connection: This psalm grounds the prayer’s confidence that God actively keeps his people in all of life, not merely in obviously religious moments.
Paul presents God as the one before whom all people are accountable, tying together God’s rule, salvation, and coming judgment.

sections.heading: Asking for hearts that can truly worship
sections.text: Give us minds shaped by your Spirit, not by the pull of our sinful nature. Make our worship, our prayers, our work, and our service pleasing to you. And make them good for us too—not empty habits, but a real sharing in the life you give.
theological_themes: Acceptable service to God flows from a Spirit-shaped mind.
The flesh resists God, while faith receives and responds to him.
God’s commands are not meant to crush his people but to lead them into life.

scripture_references.connection: Paul contrasts the mind set on the flesh with the mind set on the Spirit, which directly supports the prayer’s request to be freed from fleshly influence and made spiritually minded.
This passage connects transformed minds with worship that is offered to God in everyday life, matching the prayer’s concern that our service be acceptable to him.

sections.heading: Seeing our need and running to Christ
sections.text: Bring us into the place where we are open before you and ready to receive your love. Show us the danger we are really in when we drift from you, so that we run to you for shelter. Make us feel the sickness of our sin, so that we do not treat Jesus lightly, but value him as the Physician our souls need. Keep the cross before us until it puts to death the hostility and resistance in our hearts.
theological_themes: Awareness of danger drives sinners to God as refuge.
Sin is not merely a mistake but a deep sickness requiring Christ’s healing.
The cross reconciles sinners to God and kills our natural hostility toward him.
God’s love is received by humbled, needy people, not by the self-sufficient.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus describes his mission in terms of a physician coming for the sick, which illuminates the prayer’s image of sin as a disease and Christ as the needed healer.
Paul teaches that Christ’s blood and cross bring reconciliation and kill hostility, which directly supports the prayer’s plea that the cross would slay the enmity in our hearts.
The passage speaks of fleeing to God for refuge and holding fast to hope, matching the prayer’s request that a true sense of danger would send us to him.

sections.heading: Keeping watch over our lives
sections.text: Help us pay attention to how we live. Keep us alert to the habits we excuse, the reactions we indulge, and the motives we hide even from ourselves. When we are weak and discouraged, revive us. When we are slow and careless, wake us up. When we wander from the path, bring us back.
theological_themes: Christians are called to watchfulness over conduct, desires, and inner motives.
God restores wandering believers and revives the weary.
Sanctification includes both honest self-examination and dependence on God’s renewing mercy.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus commands watchfulness and prayer because human willingness is not enough against temptation, which fits the prayer’s plea for vigilance over our ways and hearts.
The psalm asks God to search the heart and lead the believer in the right way, grounding the prayer’s concern for hidden motives and restoration when we go astray.
David describes the Lord as the one who restores the soul and leads in right paths, which supports the prayer’s request for revival and restoration.

sections.heading: Living by faith and finding everything in Jesus
sections.text: Fill us with more of the faith that gives life to real godliness. Make us rich in faith, steady in faith, and able to live and walk by faith when sight is not enough. Let faith give us joy, strengthen our obedience, and keep hope alive in us. And when we see that we have nothing in ourselves to boast in, let us find everything we need in Jesus—our wisdom, our righteousness, our holiness, and our redemption.
theological_themes: Faith is the living root of godliness, obedience, joy, and hope.
Believers walk by faith rather than by sight.
Christ is the believer’s complete sufficiency before God.
Salvation and growth in holiness are found in Christ, not in ourselves.

scripture_references.connection: Paul’s statement that believers walk by faith rather than sight directly supports the prayer’s request to live and walk by faith.
James insists that genuine faith shows itself in action, which fits the prayer’s language about doing the work of faith rather than treating faith as mere opinion.
Paul explicitly names Christ as wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption for believers, which is the theological climax of this prayer.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase about being brought into a state that 'attracts thine eye' could be misunderstood as earning God’s love or attention. The adaptation renders it as openness before God and readiness to receive his love, preserving the Puritan concern for humility and spiritual preparedness without implying merit.

The prayer strongly contrasts 'flesh and the senses' with faith. This has been rendered as not being ruled by sinful nature, appetites, moods, or mere visible circumstances, to avoid suggesting that the created body or ordinary human senses are evil in themselves.
significant_interpretive_choices: The 'good Physician' was interpreted as Christ, in keeping with the gospel image of Jesus coming for the sick and the prayer’s movement from sin’s disease to the cross.
The phrase 'the power of faith' was rendered as living, active trust in God rather than as faith viewed as a force detached from its object.
'Jealous over our tempers' was interpreted broadly as vigilance over reactions, emotional patterns, and indulged attitudes, rather than only anger.
